Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the underlying biochemical processes that contribute to the development and
progression of osteoarthritis.
Understand the manifestations, presentation, and treatment options for osteoarthritis.
Identify high-yield testing points related to the basic science of osteoarthritis.
Pathophysiology and Pathoanatomy
Overview
OA, which eventually results in the destruction and loss of articular cartilage, is the most
prevalent disorder of the musculoskeletal system.

The disease process can progressively lead to disability via limitation of joint movement, joint
deformity, tenderness, inflammation, and severe pain.

Overview
Osteoarthritis is the most prevalent musculoskeletal disorder and results in loss of
articular cartilage. Osteoarthritis is a biochemically complex process that results from
overuse, mechanical degradation, and the generation of a local proinflammatory
environment within a joint. These processes may occur within any joint. The progressive
degeneration of cartilage causes a reactive change to the subchondral bone and the
surrounding soft tissues. Osteoarthritis typically manifests in elderly individuals. Patients
present with pain, loss of function, and characteristic radiographic findings. Resource 1
provides an excellent overview of the joint as an organ and a holistic description of
osteoarthritis.1 Video 1 provides an overview of the synovial joint.
Video 1 Grodinsky AJ: The mechanics of articular cartilage and OA, from Buckwalter JA,
mod: The synovial joint: Structure, function, injury and repair, osteoarthritis. Presented
at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans,
LA, March 6-10, 2018.

Epidemiology
The prevalence of osteoarthritis has substantially increased over the past few decades.
Osteoarthritis currently affects as many as 31 million American adults.2
The incidence of osteoarthritis increases with age, and the incidence and prevalence of
osteoarthritis vary depending on the joint involved.

Epidemiology
The true incidence and prevalence of osteoarthritis is difficult to determine and varies
across multiple studies. Several factors contribute to the inconsistencies in the reported
incidence and prevalence of osteoarthritis. The inconsistencies result from factors such
as the definition of osteoarthritis used (ie, radiographic diagnosis versus symptomatic
diagnosis), the population, and the joint studied. A general consensus among most
studies is that radiographic osteoarthritis (the presence of subchondral sclerosis, joint
space narrowing, and osteophytes) affects a considerable number of adults, and the
incidence of osteoarthritis increases with age. Because of varying factors, the prevalence
is higher in high-income countries than in low-income countries and higher in African
Americans than in Caucasians. The prevalence and severity of osteoarthritis also are
higher in women than in men.2 The incidence and prevalence of radiographic
osteoarthritis are higher than that of symptomatic osteoarthritis; it is not uncommon to
see a patient with radiographic osteoarthritis who is asymptomatic. This fact underlies
the importance of strategic clinical management by managing symptoms rather than
radiographic findings. Osteoarthritis can affect any joint, and the incidence of
osteoarthritis varies depending on the joint involved.
The global prevalence of osteoarthritis is approximately 240 million individuals, and the
incidence of hip and knee osteoarthritis was estimated to be 199 cases per 100,000
individuals by the 2016 Global Burden of Disease study. The incidence is higher in high-
income countries—347 new cases per 100,000 individuals—than in low-income
countries.2 According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, osteoarthritis
currently affects more than 32.5 million American adults. This number represents a 20%
increase from the 27 million adults diagnosed with osteoarthritis in 2005.3 The number
of osteoarthritis diagnoses is expected to increase to 67 million Americans by 2030. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603

projected rapid exponential increase is explained by the aging population and the
obesity epidemic affecting American adults.
Pathoanatomy
Cartilage
Articular cartilage is made up of the extracellular matrix (ECM; 95%) and chondrocytes (5%).4
The contents of the ECM include4
Water—It makes up a considerable portion of the articular cartilage (65% to 80%). The high
water content in the articular cartilage allows for deformation (the Young modulus of
elasticity of the articular cartilage), the inherent strength and ability of the cartilage to
support joint loads.
Collagen—Mainly type II collagen (approximately 90% to 95%) makes up 50% of the dry
weight of the articular cartilage. Collagen provides the shear and tensile strength to the
cartilage.
Proteoglycans—Secreted by chondrocytes, proteoglycans represent 10% to 15% of the dry
weight of the articular cartilage. They provide compression strength to the cartilage.
Articular cartilage is avascular and has minimal, if any, healing capacity. Osteoarthritis
develops partly because of the changes in the articular cartilage: the enzymatic degradation of
the ECM, progressive loss of articular cartilage, increased water content, and decrease in the
number of proteoglycans.5
Articular cartilage covers the ends of bones, at which they articulate with one another to
form a joint. In addition to the meniscus, synovium, and synovial fluid, it allows for smooth
and painless motion and reduces the friction and load across a joint.
Meniscus
It is made up of type I collagen.
It functions to stabilize, absorb stress, and decrease the load across the joint by increasing the
contact area within the joint.
An incompetent meniscus causes increased load and stress across the articular cartilage.

9/3/26, 5:27 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603

In symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, the meniscus is almost always incompetent from
degenerative tears (more commonly located in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus).
The degenerative tearing and displacement of the meniscus peripherally may be partly
responsible for the radiographic joint space narrowing observed in patients with osteoarthritis.
The meniscus is a peripherally vascular, fibrocartilaginous structure located in the knee joint.6
It is innervated and often is a source of articular knee pain of damaged.
Bone

Bone
In patients with osteoarthritis, the subchondral bone undergoes pathologic changes
along with the articular cartilage.7 Whether osteoarthritis develops because of the
reduced support provided to the subchondral bone by the overlying weakened and
degenerated meniscus and articular cartilage or because the subchondral bony changes
incite the articular cartilage degeneration is unclear. Regardless, as arthritis develops in
the affected joint, the subchondral bone undergoes more stress and develops
microfractures. In response, the subchondral bone attempts to remodel by forming
dense, sclerotic bone in the initial stages of osteoarthritis and bone cysts in later stages.
These changes can be observed on radiographs and represent one of the classic
radiographic characteristics of osteoarthritis. Another classic finding in patients with
osteoarthritis is the formation of periarticular osteophytes. Osteophytes are formed via
endochondral ossification by the pathologic activation of the Indian Hedgehog signaling
pathway in arthritic joints.8 The actual function of the periarticular osteophytes is
unknown; however, a working hypothesis is that they provide mechanical stability to the
arthritic joint by serving as struts supporting the joint.7 Another important contributor to
the joint pain experienced by patients with osteoarthritis is the sensory neurovascular
infiltration of the zone of calcified cartilage, the area of the cartilage immediately
adjacent to the subchondral bone. It connects the subchondral bone to the cartilage. In
nonarthritic joints, this area has poor nerve supply, but in arthritic joints, the area
experiences sensory neurovascular infiltration, causing joint pain (Figure 1; Resource 2).

Synovium
The synovium is the inner lining of the joints.
Its main function is to produce synovial fluid, which keeps the articular cartilage lubricated.
It also functions by allowing the passage of nutrients to the articular cartilage through
diffusion.
It is made up of type A and type B cells.9 Type A cells are macrophage-like cells that function by
phagocytizing foreign particles and antigens. Type B cells are fibroblast-like cells that produce
synovial fluid. In osteoarthritis, local synovitis and inflammation often are present in
combination with hyperplasia of the synovial lining cells, vascularization, and infiltration of
immune cells. This synovitis often is accompanied by periods of painful joint effusions. These
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
6/22

joint effusions contain proinflammatory cytokines that may worsen the pain and accelerate
the degenerative process at the joint.7
Pain
Pain is the primary manifestation of osteoarthritis and may be characterized as nociceptive or
neuropathic.7
Nociceptive pain is a response to local injury, mediated by the activation of nociceptive fibers
by a noxious stimulus; it is characteristically described as sharp, throbbing, and/or aching and
typically is acute in nature.
Conversely, neuropathic pain is chronic and results from central sensitization, in which
reorganization of the central and peripheral nervous systems leads to persistently activated
nociceptive pathways, even in the presence of non-noxious sensory stimuli. This pain often is
characterized as burning, tingling, and numbness.
Nociceptive and neuropathic pain may be present in patients with osteoarthritis.10 Nerve
endings are present in the synovial capsule, peripheral menisci, ligaments, periosteum, and
subchondral bone.7
Etiology

Etiology
Type II collagen helps provide the tensile and shear strength of cartilage, whereas
proteoglycans contribute to its compressive strength. Proteoglycans aggregates are
formed by the linkage of aggrecan to hyaluronic acid molecules. They interlink with
collagen fibers to form a matrix and have a net negative charge. Chondrocytes are the
only cells found in articular cartilage and are responsible for extracellular homeostasis.
In osteoarthritic cartilage, proteoglycans exist in shorter chains and characteristically
demonstrate an increased ratio of chondroitin sulfate to keratin sulfate. The total
collagen content remains the same, yet the collagen network is disordered secondary to
collagenase. The water content increases, and the modulus of elasticity and keratan
sulfate content decline.4

7/22

Natural History
Progressive degeneration typically results in worsened pain, stiffness, and potential angulation
and limb malalignment.
Risk Factors
Aging
Obesity
Genetics
Lifestyle factors
Metabolic syndrome
Intra-articular trauma
Repetitive activity

Risk Factors
The risk factors for osteoarthritis may be broadly classified as modifiable and
nonmodifiable. Modifiable risk factors include obesity and occupational/recreational
activities that lead to the mechanical overloading of joints. Nonmodifiable risk factors
include aging, female sex (postmenopause), genetics, and traumatic intra-articular
injuries.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

Patient History
In obtaining the patient history, the physician should elucidate whether the patient has a
history of intra-articular infection, fracture, or inflammatory disease. Medical
comorbidities and modifiable risk factors should be identified. Additional questions
should ascertain activities that exacerbate pain and functional limitations, theSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
8/22

effectiveness of prior treatment options, the patient’s knowledge of the disease process,
and the patient’s expectations. In the early disease stages, the severity of symptoms
often does not correlate with physical examination and imaging study findings.
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
The extent of physical examination findings is variable; however, earlier stages of
disease reveal pain with range of motion, tenderness with palpation along joint lines,
and joint effusion. Crepitation during motion and loss of motion are later findings, and
joint deformity typically is observed in later stages of disease. A ligamentous
examination should be performed to assess for articular stability and the status of
supporting collateral ligaments. Angular deformity should be identified, and it should be
noted whether the deformity is passively correctable. Because degenerative changes in
musculotendinous units around the joint are common, it essential to grade the strength
of important periarticular muscle groups, specifically the hip abductors. Observation of
the patient’s gait is an important aspect of the physical examination that needs to be
documented. Careful neurovascular examination should assess the distal pulses,
sensation, and motor strength.
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
The first imaging modality used to investigate symptomatic joints is standard plain
radiographs with orthogonal views. Although less sensitive than more advanced MRI
techniques in the early stages of disease, plain radiographs can confirm the diagnosis in
most patients.11 Although substantial joint damage may be present in the absence of
plain radiographic abnormalities, more expensive and advanced imaging modalities
should only be used if plain radiographs fail to provide adequate information (ie,-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
9/22

concern for soft-tissue pathology around the joint exists or if normal radiographic
findings prompt a high clinical suspicion for joint pathology).
Radiography
Radiographic findings
Subchondral sclerosis
Joint space narrowing
Subchondral cyst and osteophyte formation

Radiography
Radiographic technique has a considerable influence on the sensitivity of plain
radiographs in detecting evidence of arthrosis. For example, a Rosenberg view of the
knee (weight-bearing PA view in 45° of flexion) is more sensitive than a standard non–
weight-bearing AP view in detecting joint space narrowing, cysts, and osteophytes.12
Multiple classification systems are available to help stage disease radiographically,
including the Kellgren-Lawrence, Croft, and Tönnis classification systems13,14
(Resources 3 and 4). These classification systems are based on plain radiographic
assessment of joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, cyst formation,
osteophytosis, and bony deformation. In general, these classification systems are less
important for guiding treatment decisions and are most applicable for research
purposes (Tables 1 and 2).

Pathology
Biochemical changes: Enzymatic degradation of the extracellular matrix results in increased
water content and compromised resistance to mechanical insult.
Cellular changes: Chondrocyte proliferation and an increase in protease expression results in
additional matrix degradation.
Microscopic changes: Initial fibrillations within the superficial and transitional zones progress
to tidemark disruption, fissuring, remodeling, and, finally, bony eburnation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
12/22


Pathology
Early osteoarthritis is characterized by the enzymatic degradation of the ECM, with
decreased aggregan concentration and decreased proteoglycan aggregation.
Proteinases are involved in routine cartilage turnover, and matrix metalloproteinases
(collagenase, gelatinase, stromelysin) are pathologically overactive in osteoarthritis.
Disruption of the matrix integrity leads to increased water content, and the surrounding
matrix becomes less stiff and more prone to mechanical insult.4
As osteoarthritis progresses, chondrocytes respond to tissue damage by releasing
chemical mediators that increase chondrocyte proliferation. Clusters of chondrocytes
may be observed microscopically. Activation of the Wnt pathway leads to increased
expression of chondrocyte proteases. Pathologic overexpression of this pathway
promotes degradation of the cartilage matrix.
Numerous molecules have been found to be elevated in patients with osteoarthritis,
including collagenases, aggrecanases, and proinflammatory cytokines (ie, interleukin-1,
tumor necrosis factor alpha). Additional proteolytic enzymes that are pathologically
elevated include cathepsin B and D and nitric oxide synthase.4,7
In osteoarthritis, chondrocytes demonstrate a blunted response to growth factors, such
as transforming growth factor alpha and insulin-like growth factor 1, resulting in a
diminished capacity for self-repair. In healthy functioning cartilage, transforming growth
factor alpha and insulin-like growth factor 1 increase collagen and proteoglycan
synthesis while inhibiting matrix degradation, and their imbalance may promote a
catabolic environment. Proteoglycan content and keratan sulfate concentrations decline
as osteoarthritis progresses, whereas chondroitin 4-sulfate concentrations increase.4
Disruption of the fibrillar network because of the previously described changes results in
a diminished capacity for cartilage to resist compressive loads, further promoting a pro-
catabolic milieu of cytokines that leads to degenerative changes. Additional mechanical
overloading eventually leads to chondrocyte necrosis and apoptosis.4
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603

In patients with an intra-articular fracture, chondrocyte death from apoptosis may lead
to the development of posttraumatic osteoarthritis, even with anatomic reduction and
stable fixation. Chondrocyte apoptosis concentrated along fissures in the cartilage
results in the release of proteases, which lead to additional local damage.
Microscopic changes of early osteoarthritis include fibrillations within the superficial and
transition zones. Additional degeneration manifests with disruption of the tidemark,
fissuring, subchondral remodeling, and eburnation4 (Table 3 and Video 2).

Diagnosis
Macroscopic findings
Articular cartilage may show areas of softening (chondromalacia), fibrillation, and erosions.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
15/22

With severe degeneration, focal areas of ulceration may be present, with exposure of
sclerotic, eburnated subchondral bone.

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of osteoarthritis is made based on the patient history, physical
examination, and imaging studies. Currently, no role exists for routine bloodwork, and
unless concern for crystalline or septic arthropathy exists, aspiration with synovial
analysis is not routinely necessary. Radiographic findings include joint space narrowing,
osteophytosis, and subchondral sclerosis; bony deformation may be observed in
patients with end-stage disease. Macroscopic intraoperative findings of osteoarthritis
may reveal varying degrees of articular softening, fibrillation, erosions, and eburnation
(ivory-like changes to sclerotic subchondral bone).
Differential Diagnosis
Crystal arthritis—Caused by crystalline deposits (eg, uric acid, calcium pyrophosphate,
hydroxyapatite); examples include gout versus pseudogout; management involves anti-
inflammatory drugs, colchicine, dietary modifications, and management of any underlying
renal failure.
Inflammatory arthritis—Caused by an overactive immune system; examples include
rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, juvenile idiopathic
arthritis, and scleroderma; management involves immunotherapy, such as disease-modifying
antirheumatic drugs and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors.
Septic arthritis—Caused by intra-articular infection; may result from direct inoculation, spread
of adjacent infection, or hematogenous seeding; management is surgical with antibiotic
agents.
Posttraumatic arthritis—Single severe impact or repetitive high-force blunt loading may result
in chondral microdamage, chondral fracture, or osteochondral fracture; such trauma is
associated with increased chondral apoptosis; management of displaced osteochondral
fracture involves surgical reduction of displacement and stable bony fixation (Resource 5).

9/3/26, 5:27 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Strong evidence supports the following modalities:
Patient education, rehabilitation, and wellness activities
NSAID therapy (in the absence of gastric ulcers and renal dysfunction)
Elderly patients who are treated with NSAIDs should be given a proton pump inhibitor as
an adjunct to prevent gastric ulceration.
Moderate evidence supports the following:
Weight loss

Nonsurgical Management
Currently, no medical treatment options have demonstrated the ability to stop or
reverse the underlying process that leads to osteoarthritis. The nonsurgical
management of knee osteoarthritis is addressed in an American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline.
Additional treatment options include acetaminophen, physical modalities, unloader
bracing, and intra-articular viscosupplementation or corticosteroids. Except for
extenuating circumstances, the risk of narcotic agents in managing pain associated with
osteoarthritis outweighs the advantages. Using a cane in the contralateral hand is a
useful measure to offload the joint by decreasing joint reactive forces in the hip.
As the disease course progresses, patients may exhaust nonsurgical treatment
measures and request additional treatment. Corticosteroid injections frequently are
used in the management of osteoarthritis and may afford short-term pain relief.15,16
Corticosteroid injections should be used sparingly because of the potential for toxicity to
cartilage. Viscosupplementation with hyaluronic acid derivatives also has been used
successfully.17 Additional research is being conducted to develop disease-modifying
osteoarthritis drugs to prevent the progression of the disease, and several drugs
currently are being developed. Agents under investigation include intra-articular
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
17/22

capsaicin, extended-release glucocorticoids, inhibitors of the Wnt pathway, interleukin-1,
and cathepsin K.18
Cell Therapies
Investigational cell-based therapies (CBTs) may reduce inflammation and help increase the
proliferation of mesenchymal cells into connective tissues in areas of cartilage damage.

Cell Therapies
CBTs are evolving alternative treatment options for osteoarthritis. They hold exciting
promise because of the potential for reversing or stabilizing osteoarthritis and provide a
less invasive and less expensive alternative to surgical management.19 Platelet-rich
plasma and stromal cells are among the most common forms of injectable CBT currently
used to manage osteoarthritis. These therapies are thought to affect symptoms via a
paracrine mechanism by producing anti-inflammatory mediators. They also may help to
increase the proliferation and differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells into
connective tissue cells in areas of tissue damage.19 The end result of CBT management is
to restore lost or damaged articular cartilage and provide pain relief while improving
function. The current limitations to CBT include the unknown long-term effects and a
lack of standardization in its processing and delivery. In addition, a paucity of well-
conducted randomized controlled trials have shown the clear superior efficacy of
CBTs.19 (Resource 6)
Surgical Management

Surgical Management
After nonsurgical treatment options have been exhausted, surgical management may be
indicated to improve pain, maintain mobility, and maximize function. Various surgical
techniques have been described, depending on the patient’s age, activity, desired level of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:27 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000603
18/22

function, and associated comorbidities. A discussion of each surgical option for the
management of osteoarthritis is beyond the scope of this lesson, and additional learning
should be tailored to the particular joint of interest. Broadly, the goals of surgical
management of osteoarthritis are to remove the arthritic segment and implant a new
articulation with stable fixation and restored biomechanics to allow for early motion.
Outcomes vary, depending on the particular joint and technique used. Some procedures,
such as total elbow arthroplasty, may be associated with a lifelong weight-bearing
restriction for the managed limb. Complications may result because of infection,
periprosthetic fracture, loosening, osteolysis, and stiffness. The authors of this lesson
recommend additional study focused on the joint of interest to explore the particular
indications, contraindications, techniques, pearls, outcomes, and complications
associated with the surgical management of osteoarthritis.
Mark as Complete
